extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and policymakers interested in church–state relations, political philosophy, and 19th-century public controversy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying normative criteria and argumentative standards used to assess claims about the relation of Church and State, the right of private judgment, and the proper ends and actions of government. Focuses on historical evidence, institutional unity, and pragmatic policy limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary end of Government
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary (main) end of Government is a purely temporal end: the protection of the persons and property of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government should be constructed with a single view to that main end; other objectives are secondary and must not impair the Government's efficiency in protecting persons and property. (Analogy: specialized tools perform their main task better than multi-purpose ones.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize government solely for its main end
rubrics_metrics.description: Government should be organised solely with a view to its main end and not sacrifice any part of its efficiency for that end to promote other ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While other good ends may be desirable, they must not reduce the state's ability to perform its primary function. Examples: a hospital's wards should not be compromised for architectural splendour; likewise, state institutions should not be shaped to pursue extraneous aims at the cost of their core purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible pursuit of collateral ends
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Government can, without any sacrifice of its main end, pursue other good (collateral) ends, it ought to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated examples include patronage of the arts, national galleries, publication of archives, libraries, menageries, scientific voyages. The test is pragmatic: pursue collateral ends only when they do not impair the main purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote useful means subordinate to main end
rubrics_metrics.description: The state ought to promote things that, while not primary ends, are useful means to secure the main end (e.g., improvements in steam navigation because they aid national defence and cohesion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such promotion is justified when the means demonstrably enhance the state's capacity to achieve its primary functions (defence, communication, consolidation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic tolerance of mixed truth and error in state-supported institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: No human machinery for promoting truth is perfect; some alloy of error is inevitable when the state supports religious instruction or institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy must accept a degree of imperfection and be guided by circumstances: e.g., it may be wrong to fund Jesuit missions among Protestants, but permissible to fund Catholic ministers ministering to isolated Catholic soldiers; weigh harms and benefits case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: State support for diverse religious ministers where it serves individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible for the State to provide or fund ministers of a religion different from the majority when this serves the spiritual needs of individuals (e.g., sending a Catholic confessor to an isolated Catholic soldier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical compassion for individuals and fulfilment of obligations to servants/soldiers can justify such support; the personal obligations of masters and the state's duty to those who serve it are invoked as moral grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency principle for public funding of religion
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is wrong to fund those who teach false doctrine, that principle applies equally to grants for ministers of the Established Church when they may teach false doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues for consistent application: the mere fact of establishment should not exempt a body from scrutiny about doctrinal truth; funding decisions must consider the real diversity of teaching within recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity as essential to institutional claim to truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of doctrine is essential to the claim of an institution (like a Church) to be the vehicle of truth; lack of unity undermines such a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to the Church of England: its formularies and practice admit wide theological latitude, so its professed unity is more nominal than substantive; therefore unity cannot be invoked as proof of truth or authoritative teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of historical evidence for apostolical succession
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that a Church has an unbroken apostolical succession requires very strong historical evidence because many contingencies could have interrupted succession across centuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of gaps and obscurities in early and medieval ecclesiastical history (e.g., illiteracy, corrupt appointments, possible impostors, sold sees), the absence of decisive contemporary testimony means one should require robust proof before accepting succession as a basis for authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostolical succession does not prove doctrinal truth by itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if apostolical succession were proven, it would not in itself make the doctrines taught more true; truth does not gain truthfulness by being handed down in an unbroken series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Nicene faith is not truer when proclaimed by a high prelate than by a lay moderator; authority derived from succession must still be judged by the truth of doctrines themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protestant clarification of private judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Protestant doctrine of the right of private judgment does not assert that opposing opinions are equally true or harmless; rather it asserts there is no visible body whose decrees bind private judgment on points of faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects caricatures (that Protestants claim truth and falsehood can both be true) and emphasizes that Protestants still value truth and denounce error; their position is about the absence of an authoritative external body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of free inquiry: unity in exact sciences vs discrepancy in moral/religious matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Free inquiry tends to produce unity in the exact sciences (e.g., mathematics) but leads to persistent discrepancy in moral and religious questions because of the constitution of the human mind and the nature of moral evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore some discrepancy is inevitable even among diligent and candid inquirers; such discrepancy can be interpreted as an index of active public engagement rather than as evidence that inquiry is harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two coherent policy responses to private judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two intelligible consistent courses regarding private judgment: the Romanist course which forbids private judgment to secure repose; and the Protestant course which permits private judgment despite its inevitable inconveniences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both are presented as reasonable positions; the critique is directed at attempting to have private judgment without accepting its consequences (unity without accepting the discrepancy that follows from free inquiry).
